'''Aviv Regev''' ({{lang|he|אביב רגב}}; born 11 July 1971) is an Israeli-American computational and systems biologist whose research has focused on gene-regulatory networks, [[single-cell genomics]], and the application of machine learning to biology and drug discovery. She is Head and Executive Vice President of [[Genentech]] Research and Early Development (gRED) and a member of the enlarged Corporate Executive Committee of [[Roche]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr Aviv Regev |url=https://www.roche.com/about/leadership/aviv-regev |website=Roche |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref>

Regev pioneered experimental and computational approaches in single-cell genomics, helping establish methods for identifying cell types and states, reconstructing cellular organization in tissues, and studying gene-regulatory circuits at single-cell resolution.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Nowogrodzki |first=Anna |title=The cell seeker |journal=Nature |volume=547 |pages=24–26 |year=2017 |doi=10.1038/547024a}}</ref> In 2016, she and [[Sarah Teichmann]] co-founded the [[Human Cell Atlas]], an international effort to create comprehensive reference maps of the cells in the human body.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rozenblatt-Rosen |first1=Orit |last2=Stubbington |first2=Michael J. T. |last3=Regev |first3=Aviv |last4=Teichmann |first4=Sarah A. |title=The Human Cell Atlas: from vision to reality |journal=Nature |volume=550 |pages=451–453 |year=2017 |doi=10.1038/550451a}}</ref> More recently, she has developed what she calls the "Lab in the Loop", an approach that iteratively combines large-scale biological experiments with machine-learning models to guide subsequent experiments and drug discovery.<ref>{{cite web |title=Aviv Regev on Design for Inference: From Random Experiments to Lab in the Loop |url=https://datascience.stanford.edu/events/distinguished-lecture/aviv-regev-design-inference-random-experiments-lab-loop |website=Stanford Data Science |date=5 June 2024 |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref>

Before joining Genentech in 2020, Regev was a professor of biology at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], a core member and chair of the faculty at the [[Broad Institute]], founding director of its Klarman Cell Observatory, and an investigator at the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr Aviv Regev |url=https://www.roche.com/about/leadership/aviv-regev |website=Roche |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref>

==Education==
Regev studied at the [[Adi Lautman Interdisciplinary Program for Outstanding Students]] of [[Tel Aviv University]], where she completed her PhD under the supervision of [[Eva Jablonka]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Regev|first1=A.|last2=Lamb|first2=M. J.|last3=Jablonka|first3=E.|date=1998|title=The Role of DNA Methylation in Invertebrates: Developmental Regulation or Genome Defense?|journal=[[Molecular Biology and Evolution]]|volume=15|issue=7|page=880|doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.molbev.a025992|issn=0737-4038|doi-access=free}}</ref> and [[Ehud Shapiro]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Regev | first1 = A. | last2 = Shapiro | first2 = E. | title = Cellular abstractions: Cells as computation | journal = Nature | volume = 419 | issue = 6905 | page = 343 | year = 2002 | doi = 10.1038/419343a| pmid = 12353013 | pmc = 3842595 | bibcode = 2002Natur.419..343R }} {{closed access}}</ref>

==Career and research==

Regev's research has centered on using computational approaches to understand how molecular and cellular systems are organized and regulated. During her doctoral work, she investigated whether concepts from theoretical computer science could be used to model biological systems, applying [[pi-calculus]], a formalism developed for describing interacting computational processes, to biochemical networks.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Regev |first1=Aviv |last2=Shapiro |first2=Ehud |title=Cellular abstractions: Cells as computation |journal=Nature |volume=419 |page=343 |year=2002 |doi=10.1038/419343a}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sansom |first1=Clare |last2=Morrison McKay |first2=B. J. |title=ISCB Honors David Haussler and Aviv Regev |journal=PLOS Computational Biology |volume=4 |issue=7 |year=2008 |doi=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000101  |doi-access=free|pmid=18795145|pmc=2536508 }}</ref> After completing her Ph.D. in 2002, she became a Bauer Fellow at Harvard University's Center for Genomics Research, where she established an independent research group and began using genomic and gene-expression data to reconstruct gene-regulatory networks.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sansom |first1=Clare |last2=Morrison McKay |first2=B. J. |title=ISCB Honors David Haussler and Aviv Regev |journal=PLOS Computational Biology |volume=4 |issue=7 |year=2008 |doi=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000101  |doi-access=free|pmid=18795145|pmc=2536508 }}</ref> This work included the development, with collaborators, of "module networks", a probabilistic approach for identifying groups of co-regulated genes and their candidate regulators from gene-expression data.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Segal |first1=Eran |last2=Shapira |first2=Michael |last3=Regev |first3=Aviv |last4=Pe'er |first4=Dana |last5=Botstein |first5=David |last6=Koller |first6=Daphne |last7=Friedman |first7=Nir |title=Module networks: identifying regulatory modules and their condition-specific regulators from gene expression data |journal=Nature Genetics |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=166–176 |year=2003 |doi=10.1038/ng1165 |pmid=12740579}}</ref>

In 2006, Regev joined the faculty of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and became a core member of the [[Broad Institute]]. Her research there combined computational modeling with experimental biology to study how cellular regulatory circuits respond to genetic and environmental changes, with applications including immune-cell differentiation, cancer and evolution.<ref>{{cite journal |title=2017 ISCB Innovator Award: Aviv Regev |journal=PLOS Computational Biology |volume=13 |issue=6 |year=2017 |doi=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005640 |doi-access=free|pmc=5542674 }}</ref> In 2012, she became the founding director of the Broad Institute's Klarman Cell Observatory, established to develop systematic experimental and computational approaches for studying cellular circuits and their roles in health and disease.<ref>{{cite web |title=Klarman Cell Observatory |website=Broad Institute |url=https://www.broadinstitute.org/klarman-cell-observatory |access-date=16 September 2026}}</ref> She subsequently served as director of the Broad's Cell Circuits Program and, from 2014 to 2020, as chair of its faculty.<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr Aviv Regev |website=Roche |url=https://www.roche.com/about/leadership/aviv-regev |access-date=16 September 2026}}</ref>

Her work increasingly focused on single-cell genomics, using measurements from individual cells to identify cell types and states and to infer the regulatory programs that control them.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nowogrodzki |first1=Anna |title=The cell seeker |journal=Nature |volume=547 |pages=24–26 |year=2017 |doi=10.1038/547024a}}</ref> In 2016, Regev and [[Sarah Teichmann]] co-founded the [[Human Cell Atlas]], an international initiative to create comprehensive reference maps of the cells in the human body. The project was launched with approximately 100 scientists and grew into a global consortium using single-cell and spatial genomic technologies to characterize human tissues in health and disease.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Human Cell Atlas is a remarkable achievement |journal=Nature |volume=635 |year=2024 |doi=10.1038/d41586-024-03754-y|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In August 2020, Regev joined [[Genentech]] as head and executive vice president of Genentech Research and Early Development (gRED), with responsibility for the company's research and early drug-development organization, and became a member of Roche's enlarged Corporate Executive Committee.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Mullard |first=Asher |title=Aviv Regev |journal=Nature Reviews Drug Discovery |volume=20 |pages=256–257 |year=2021 |doi=10.1038/d41573-021-00051-5}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Dr Aviv Regev |website=Roche |url=https://www.roche.com/about/leadership/aviv-regev |access-date=16 September 2026}}</ref> She has continued to lead research combining experimental methods, large-scale biological measurements and computational approaches to study cellular circuits, while applying these approaches to drug discovery and development.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Mullard |first=Asher |title=Aviv Regev |journal=Nature Reviews Drug Discovery |volume=20 |pages=256–257 |year=2021 |doi=10.1038/d41573-021-00051-5}}</ref>

=== Single Cell Genomics ===
Regev pioneered single-cell genomics, developing experimental and computational approaches for using single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize cellular identity, variation, and gene-regulatory programs in complex tissues.<ref>{{cite web |title=Aviv Regev |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/aviv-regev |website=American Academy of Arts and Sciences |access-date=15 September 2026}}</ref> Her group applied these methods to problems ranging from immune responses to cancer, helping show how single-cell measurements could reveal distinct cell states and molecular programs that are obscured when cells are analyzed in bulk.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Shalek |first=Alex K. |title=Single-cell transcriptomics reveals bimodality in expression and splicing in immune cells |journal=Nature |volume=498 |pages=236–240 |year=2013 |doi=10.1038/nature12172 |pmid=23685454|pmc=3683364 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Tirosh |first=Itay |title=Dissecting the multicellular ecosystem of metastatic melanoma by single-cell RNA-seq |journal=Science |volume=352 |issue=6282 |pages=189–196 |year=2016 |doi=10.1126/science.aad0501 |pmid=27124452|pmc=4944528 }}</ref> Regev and collaborators also developed computational methods for reconstructing the spatial organization of cells from single-cell gene-expression data,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Satija |first=Rahul |author2=Farrell, Jeffrey A. |author3=Gennert, David |author4=Schier, Alexander F. |author5=Regev, Aviv |title=Spatial reconstruction of single-cell gene expression data |journal=Nature Biotechnology |volume=33 |pages=495–502 |year=2015 |doi=10.1038/nbt.3192|pmc=4430369 }}</ref> and co-developed Perturb-seq, which combines pooled CRISPR-based genetic perturbations with single-cell RNA sequencing to measure how genetic changes affect gene expression across individual cells.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Dixit |first=Atray |title=Perturb-Seq: Dissecting Molecular Circuits with Scalable Single-Cell RNA Profiling of Pooled Genetic Screens |journal=Cell |volume=167 |issue=7 |pages=1853–1866.e17 |year=2016 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2016.11.038 |pmid=27984732|pmc=5181115 }}</ref> This work helped extend single-cell genomics from cataloguing cell types and states to probing the regulatory mechanisms that control them,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Tanay |first=Amos |author2=Regev, Aviv |title=Scaling single-cell genomics from phenomenology to mechanism |journal=Nature |volume=541 |pages=331–338 |year=2017 |doi=10.1038/nature21350 |pmid=28102262|pmc=5438464 }}</ref> and contributed to the scientific basis for large-scale efforts to map human cells, including the Human Cell Atlas.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Nowogrodzki |first=Anna |title=The cell seeker |journal=Nature |volume=547 |pages=24–26 |date=6 July 2017 |doi=10.1038/547024a}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Rozenblatt-Rosen |first=Orit |author2=Stubbington, Michael J. T. |author3=Regev, Aviv |author4=Teichmann, Sarah A. |title=The Human Cell Atlas: from vision to reality |journal=Nature |volume=550 |pages=451–453 |year=2017 |doi=10.1038/550451a |pmid=29072289}}</ref>

=== Human Cell Atlas ===

In 2016, Regev and British computational biologist [[Sarah Teichmann]] co-founded the [[Human Cell Atlas]] (HCA), an international initiative to create comprehensive reference maps of the cells in the human body.<ref>{{cite journal |title=A ‘Wikipedia for cells’: researchers get an updated look at the Human Cell Atlas, and it’s remarkable |journal=Nature |date=20 November 2024 |doi=10.1038/d41586-024-03754-y|doi-access=free }}</ref> The project was launched with around 100 scientists and aimed to catalogue human cell types and states across tissues, stages of development and age, using rapidly developing single-cell genomic technologies.<ref>{{cite journal |title=A ‘Wikipedia for cells’: researchers get an updated look at the Human Cell Atlas, and it’s remarkable |journal=Nature |date=20 November 2024 |doi=10.1038/d41586-024-03754-y|doi-access=free }}</ref> Regev and Teichmann served as co-chairs of the project's organizing committee, helping define its scientific goals, organizational structure and approach to creating an openly accessible reference atlas.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rozenblatt-Rosen |first1=Orit |last2=Stubbington |first2=Michael J. T. |last3=Regev |first3=Aviv |last4=Teichmann |first4=Sarah A. |title=The Human Cell Atlas: from vision to reality |journal=Nature |volume=550 |pages=451–453 |year=2017 |doi=10.1038/550451a}}</ref>

The HCA extended the use of single-cell genomics from studying individual tissues or biological questions to systematically mapping cellular diversity throughout the human body. As single-cell and [[spatial transcriptomics|spatial genomic]] technologies developed, the project expanded beyond a census of cell types to map where cells are located in tissues, how they change during development, and how molecular and genetic variation is related to cell state and disease.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rood |first1=Jennifer E. |last2=Wynne |first2=Samantha |last3=Robson |first3=Lucia |last4=Hupalowska |first4=Anna |last5=Randell |first5=John |last6=Teichmann |first6=Sarah A. |last7=Regev |first7=Aviv |title=The Human Cell Atlas from a cell census to a unified foundation model |journal=Nature |volume=637 |pages=1065–1071 |year=2025 |doi=10.1038/s41586-024-08338-4}}</ref> By 2024, the consortium had entered a data-integration phase aimed at producing a first draft Human Cell Atlas organized around 18 biological networks covering major organs and systems.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Human Cell Atlas: towards a first draft atlas |url=https://www.nature.com/collections/jccbbdahji |website=Nature |date=20 November 2024 |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref>

=== Artificial intelligence and lab in the loop ===

Regev's research has increasingly focused on combining [[machine learning]] with large-scale experimental biology to make biological research and drug discovery more predictive. An early formulation of this approach was "design for inference": because the number of possible genetic perturbations, cellular states and therapeutic interventions is too large to measure exhaustively, experiments can instead be designed to generate informative data from which computational models infer unmeasured possibilities and guide subsequent experiments.<ref>{{cite web |title=MLCB 2020 Schedule |url=https://sites.google.com/cs.washington.edu/mlcb2020/schedule |website=Machine Learning in Computational Biology |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref> Regev presented this approach in a 2020 keynote at the Machine Learning in Computational Biology meeting titled "Design for Inference for Tissue Biology", and subsequently in an invited talk at the [[International Conference on Machine Learning]] (ICML) in 2022 titled "Design for Inference in Drug Discovery and Development".<ref>{{cite web |title=ICML 2022 Invited Talks |url=https://icml.cc/virtual/2022/events/invited%20talk |website=International Conference on Machine Learning |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref>

At [[Genentech]], Regev has developed this idea into what she describes as a "Lab in the Loop", an iterative framework in which experimental or clinical data are used to train artificial-intelligence models, the models make predictions or propose new experiments and molecular designs, and the results of those experiments are then used to improve the models.<ref>{{cite web |title=Aviv Regev on Design for Inference: From Random Experiments to Lab in the Loop |url=https://datascience.stanford.edu/events/distinguished-lecture/aviv-regev-design-inference-random-experiments-lab-loop |website=Stanford Data Science |date=5 June 2024 |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref> She has described the framework as applicable across multiple stages of drug research and development, including understanding disease biology, identifying therapeutic targets, designing medicines and predicting which treatments may benefit particular patients.<ref>{{cite news |last=Mullard |first=Asher |title=Aviv Regev |journal=Nature Reviews Drug Discovery |volume=20 |pages=256–257 |year=2021 |doi=10.1038/d41573-021-00051-5}}</ref>

Regev has presented this approach at major scientific and technology conferences. At [[TED (conference)|TED]]AI in 2023, in a talk titled "Can AI help develop new medicines?", she described using AI to analyze large biological datasets and improve the process of developing medicines.<ref>{{cite web |title=Can AI help develop new medicines? |url=https://www.ted.com/talks/aviv_regev_can_ai_help_develop_new_medicines |website=TED |date=October 2023 |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref> She also presented the Lab in the Loop framework at NVIDIA's GTC conference and in a Stanford Data Science Distinguished Lecture in 2024,<ref>{{cite web |title=Lab in a Loop: AI to Transform Drug Discovery and Development |url=https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/on-demand/session/gtc24-s62281/ |website=NVIDIA |date=March 2024 |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref> and returned to ICML as an invited speaker in 2026, where her talk focused on applying the approach across drug research and development.<ref>{{cite web |last=Kamath |first=Gautam |title=Announcing the ICML 2026 Invited Talks |url=https://blog.icml.cc/2026/05/18/announcing-the-icml-2026-invited-talks/ |website=ICML Blog |date=18 May 2026 |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref> In a 2026 interview with ''[[Scientific American]]'', Regev described extending this strategy toward generative-AI models that can infer unmeasured biological information, guide the collection of new data and contribute to predictive "virtual cell" models of cellular behavior.<ref>{{cite news |last=Nuwer |first=Rachel |title=Aviv Regev on how generative AI is becoming the new language of science |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/aviv-regev/ |work=Scientific American |date=16 June 2026 |access-date=17 September 2026}}</ref>
